title: The Case of the Damp Bottom Shelf
story: Forty books on the bottom shelf of the north wall have swollen covers and wavy pages. The damage is worst at the wall end of the shelf and fades along it. Books on the top shelf, directly under the roof, are dry and flat. A roof leak runs downward, so the top shelf would be the wet one. The room's humidity reads forty-four percent, which is normal for the building. Air that damp would affect every shelf in the room equally, and it has not. A spilled bottle soaks one patch and leaves the books beside it untouched. This damage runs along four metres of shelving in a single gradient. The plaster behind that shelf is blistered from the skirting board upward. A hot water pipe runs inside the north wall at floor level. Water escaping at floor level wets what sits lowest and nearest, which is exactly the pattern on the shelf. The cleaning crew have not mopped that aisle since the damage was reported.
q: What is wetting the books?

sus.why: a hot water pipe runs inside the north wall at floor level
a roof leak runs downward, so the top shelf would be the wet one
air that damp would affect every shelf in the room equally, and it has not
a spilled bottle soaks one patch and leaves the books beside it untouched
the cleaning crew have not mopped that aisle since the damage was reported

proof: “The plaster behind that shelf is blistered from the skirting board upward.”

“The damage is worst at the wall end of the shelf and fades along it.”
clears: A roof leak: “Books on the top shelf, directly under the roof, are dry and flat.”
Humidity: “The room's humidity reads forty-four percent, which is normal for the building.”
A bottle: “This damage runs along four metres of shelving in a single gradient.”
The cleaners: “The cleaning crew have not mopped that aisle since the damage was reported.”
explain: Each suspect predicts a shape. A roof leak predicts damage from the top down, humidity predicts it everywhere at once, a bottle predicts one patch. The shape on the shelf is lowest and nearest a wall, which is the only prediction left standing, and the blistered plaster confirms it.

title: The Case of the Friday Sandwich
story: Mira's sandwich is slimy on Fridays and fine the other four days of the week. The bread comes from one loaf bought on Sunday and used all week. If the bread were the problem, Thursday's sandwich would be worse than Monday's. The deli meat is sliced fresh on Thursday evening for Friday only. Meat sliced the night before would spoil in the refrigerator too, and it does not. The mayonnaise jar is opened on Monday and used every day from the same spoon. Mayonnaise would affect every sandwich in the week, not one of them. The lunchbox is washed in hot water on Thursday night after school. It is dried with a cloth and the lid is clipped shut while the seams are still wet. A sealed box with water trapped in its seams grows a film overnight. Thursday is the only night the box is both washed and closed. A box left open on the rack on other nights is dry by morning.
q: Why is the Friday sandwich slimy?

sus.who: 📦 The box clipped shut while wet
sus.why: it is dried with a cloth and the lid is clipped shut while the seams are still wet
if the bread were the problem, Thursday's sandwich would be worse than Monday's
meat sliced the night before would spoil in the refrigerator too, and it does not
mayonnaise would affect every sandwich in the week, not one of them
a box left open on the rack on other nights is dry by morning

ans: The lunchbox is clipped shut on Thursday night with water in its seams.
proof: “A sealed box with water trapped in its seams grows a film overnight.”
“Thursday is the only night the box is both washed and closed.”
“A box left open on the rack on other nights is dry by morning.”

The meat: “Meat sliced the night before would spoil in the refrigerator too, and it does not.”
The mayonnaise: “Mayonnaise would affect every sandwich in the week, not one of them.”
The wash: “A box left open on the rack on other nights is dry by morning.”
explain: Three of the four food suspects are ruled out by a prediction about other days: each would spoil more than one sandwich a week. Washing is not the fault either, since the box is washed on other nights too. What happens only on Thursday is washing and closing in the same move.

title: The Case of the Breaking Leads
story: Pencils from the new box snap their points within a word or two of sharpening. Pencils from the old box sharpen in the same sharpener and write all period. If the sharpener's blade were dull, pencils from both boxes would break. The two boxes are the same brand and the same HB grade, printed on the barrel. A softer grade would smudge as well as snap, and these do not smudge at all. Pressing hard would break points for one student and not for a whole class. Every student using the new box reports the same thing within a day. A pencil's lead is one thin rod running the full length of the barrel. A sharp knock cracks that rod in several places without marking the wood. Each crack becomes a break as soon as the sharpener exposes it. The new box arrived in a carton the delivery driver dropped on the step. The old box has sat on the shelf since September and has not been moved.
q: Why do the new pencils keep snapping?

sus.why: the new box arrived in a carton the delivery driver dropped on the step
if the sharpener's blade were dull, pencils from both boxes would break
a softer grade would smudge as well as snap, and these do not smudge at all
pressing hard would break points for one student and not for a whole class
a sharp knock cracks that rod in several places without marking the wood

ans: The dropped carton cracked the leads inside the new pencils.
proof: “A sharp knock cracks that rod in several places without marking the wood.”
“Each crack becomes a break as soon as the sharpener exposes it.”
“The new box arrived in a carton the delivery driver dropped on the step.”
clears: The sharpener: “If the sharpener's blade were dull, pencils from both boxes would break.”
The grade: “A softer grade would smudge as well as snap, and these do not smudge at all.”
Pressing: “Every student using the new box reports the same thing within a day.”
The wood: “A sharp knock cracks that rod in several places without marking the wood.”
explain: The old box is the control for the sharpener, the printed grade is the control for the lead, and a whole class is the control for pressing. What is left is a box that was dropped, and a lead that can be broken in six places while the pencil still looks perfect.

title: The Case of the Bowl That Ripened
story: Five apples in the kitchen bowl went soft and brown within four days of being picked. Six apples from the same tree, left in a dish on the counter, are still firm. The two groups were picked on the same morning from the same branch. A bad batch would have gone soft in the dish as well as in the bowl. Bruising shows as a brown patch where the fruit was struck, not as softening throughout. None of the five carries a mark on its skin anywhere. The bowl is wood and the dish is china, and neither reacts with fruit. The bowl also held two bananas that were spotted brown when the apples went in. Ripening fruit gives off ethylene gas, which ripens other fruit near it. Gas pools in a deep bowl and disperses from a shallow dish. Two pears that shared the bowl have gone soft as well, and the pears in the dish are hard.
q: What ripened the apples?

sus.why: the bowl also held two bananas that were spotted brown when the apples went in
a bad batch would have gone soft in the dish as well as in the bowl
none of the five carries a mark on its skin anywhere
the bowl is wood and the dish is china, and neither reacts with fruit
the two groups were picked on the same morning from the same branch

ans: Ethylene from the bananas ripened everything in the bowl.
proof: “Ripening fruit gives off ethylene gas, which ripens other fruit near it.”
“Gas pools in a deep bowl and disperses from a shallow dish.”
“Two pears that shared the bowl have gone soft as well, and the pears in the dish are hard.”
clears: A bad batch: “A bad batch would have gone soft in the dish as well as in the bowl.”
Bruising: “None of the five carries a mark on its skin anywhere.”
The bowl: “The bowl is wood and the dish is china, and neither reacts with fruit.”
The tree: “The two groups were picked on the same morning from the same branch.”
explain: The pears are the test that separates the last two explanations. Something about the fruit itself would not touch a pear, and something about the bowl would not have spared the dish. A gas that fills a bowl ripens whatever is in it, pears included.

title: The Case of the Wheel That Would Not Stay True
story: The rear wheel pulls out of true within a week of every truing, and the front wheel never does. Both wheels run the same roads, the same potholes and the same rider. If potholes were the cause, the front wheel would go out first and harder. The rim was checked for cracks and dents and is straight when the spokes are even. A cracked rim would hold a bend in one place rather than drifting slowly. The hub bearings spin smoothly and have no play when the wheel is rocked. The same two spokes are loose at every truing, and both are on the chain side. A rear wheel is dished, so its chain-side spokes pull at a steeper angle. Spokes at a steeper angle carry more tension and lose it first if they were set low. Tension was measured after the last truing and those two read well under the others. Nothing on the front wheel is dished, which is why nothing on it moves.

sus.why: tension was measured after the last truing and those two read well under the others
if potholes were the cause, the front wheel would go out first and harder
a cracked rim would hold a bend in one place rather than drifting slowly
the hub bearings spin smoothly and have no play when the wheel is rocked
both wheels run the same roads, the same potholes and the same rider

ans: Two chain-side spokes were left at low tension and keep letting go.
proof: “A rear wheel is dished, so its chain-side spokes pull at a steeper angle.”
“Spokes at a steeper angle carry more tension and lose it first if they were set low.”

The rim: “A cracked rim would hold a bend in one place rather than drifting slowly.”
The bearings: “The hub bearings spin smoothly and have no play when the wheel is rocked.”
The rider: “Both wheels run the same roads, the same potholes and the same rider.”
explain: The front wheel is the control for everything the bike meets: same roads, same rider, same potholes, and it stays true. The difference is inside the rear wheel, where dishing puts the chain-side spokes under more load, and the same two keep failing because they were never brought up to tension.

title: The Case of the Algae on One Pane
story: Green film coats the left pane of the tank and leaves the other three clear. Overfeeding raises nutrients in the water, and water circulates past every pane equally. Nutrients in the water would green all four sides rather than one. The tap water was tested for phosphate and came back at almost nothing. Phosphate would also feed algae everywhere the water touches, which is everywhere. The tank's own lamp sits centred above it and lights all four panes the same. The left pane faces a west window about a metre away. Algae need light, and more light on one surface grows more algae there. The green stops in a sharp horizontal line two thirds of the way up the pane. A shelf above the window casts a shadow across the tank at exactly that height. The film is thickest at the end of weeks with clear afternoons. Scraping the pane clean leaves it green again within nine or ten days.
q: Why is only one pane green?

sus.who: 🪟 Afternoon light from the west window
sus.why: the left pane faces a west window about a metre away
nutrients in the water would green all four sides rather than one
the tap water was tested for phosphate and came back at almost nothing
the tank's own lamp sits centred above it and lights all four panes the same
overfeeding raises nutrients in the water, and water circulates past every pane equally

ans: Window light on the left pane is growing the algae there.
proof: “Algae need light, and more light on one surface grows more algae there.”
“The green stops in a sharp horizontal line two thirds of the way up the pane.”
“A shelf above the window casts a shadow across the tank at exactly that height.”
clears: Overfeeding: “Nutrients in the water would green all four sides rather than one.”
Phosphate: “The tap water was tested for phosphate and came back at almost nothing.”
The lamp: “The tank's own lamp sits centred above it and lights all four panes the same.”
The filter: “Overfeeding raises nutrients in the water, and water circulates past every pane equally.”
explain: Anything carried in the water reaches all four panes, so a one-sided problem cannot be a water problem. The shadow line is the proof: the algae stop exactly where the light stops, which no nutrient could arrange.

title: The Case of the Cabinet That Buzzed
story: A hard buzz comes from the display cabinet whenever the projector runs, and stops the moment it is switched off. The projector itself hums steadily and that hum is a different, softer sound. A loose cabinet screw would buzz when anything shook the room, including footsteps. Walking heavily past the cabinet produces no sound at all. The buzz only happens at the projector's high fan speed and never at the low one. Every object has a frequency at which it vibrates easily, and a push at that rate sets it going. The glass shelf inside the cabinet rests loose in its brackets at both ends. Laying a folded cloth under one end of that shelf silences the buzz completely. Removing the cloth brings the buzz back on the next high-speed run. The radiator was off all week and the buzz happened anyway. The cabinet door latch was tightened on Monday and made no difference.
q: What is buzzing?

sus.why: the glass shelf inside the cabinet rests loose in its brackets at both ends
walking heavily past the cabinet produces no sound at all
the projector itself hums steadily and that hum is a different, softer sound
the radiator was off all week and the buzz happened anyway
the cabinet door latch was tightened on Monday and made no difference

ans: The loose glass shelf vibrates at the projector's high fan speed.
proof: “Every object has a frequency at which it vibrates easily, and a push at that rate sets it going.”
“Laying a folded cloth under one end of that shelf silences the buzz completely.”
“Removing the cloth brings the buzz back on the next high-speed run.”
clears: A loose screw: “Walking heavily past the cabinet produces no sound at all.”
The projector: “The projector itself hums steadily and that hum is a different, softer sound.”
The radiator: “The radiator was off all week and the buzz happened anyway.”
The latch: “The cabinet door latch was tightened on Monday and made no difference.”
explain: The cloth is the experiment that settles it, and it is run twice: in and the buzz stops, out and the buzz returns. The high fan speed matters because only one speed pushes at the rate the shelf answers to.

args.against: “The buzz only happens at the projector's high fan speed and never at the low one.”

The door latch: “Monday's tightening of the door latch changed nothing at all.”
d.note: The cloth is a proper experiment run in both directions: in, silence, out, buzz. That is the strongest evidence any of these cases offers. The other two answers have to explain why a cloth under a shelf stops a buzz coming from a back panel or a bracket.

title: The Case of the Sticky Leaves
story: The young leaves at the tips of the lime tree are curled, and the path beneath it is sticky. Drought curls leaves from the edges inward and leaves nothing sticky behind. The tree has been watered twice a week and the soil is damp a spade deep. Leaf diseases usually show as spots or patches with a clear edge. The curled leaves have no spots and are an even green underneath the curl. Salt damage browns leaf margins, and these margins are not browned. Aphids feed on new growth and excrete a sugary liquid called honeydew. Honeydew falls on whatever is below, which is why the path is tacky. Ants farm aphids for that honeydew and carry them to fresh shoots. A steady column of ants runs up the trunk and out along the tip branches. Curling is confined to this year's shoots and none of the older leaves are affected.
q: What is wrong with the lime tree?

sus.why: aphids feed on new growth and excrete a sugary liquid called honeydew
the tree has been watered twice a week and the soil is damp a spade deep
the curled leaves have no spots and are an even green underneath the curl
salt damage browns leaf margins, and these margins are not browned
curling is confined to this year's shoots and none of the older leaves are affected

ans: Aphids are feeding on the new shoots and dripping honeydew.
proof: “Honeydew falls on whatever is below, which is why the path is tacky.”
“Ants farm aphids for that honeydew and carry them to fresh shoots.”
“A steady column of ants runs up the trunk and out along the tip branches.”
clears: Drought: “The tree has been watered twice a week and the soil is damp a spade deep.”
Disease: “The curled leaves have no spots and are an even green underneath the curl.”
Salt: “Salt damage browns leaf margins, and these margins are not browned.”
Old leaves: “Curling is confined to this year's shoots and none of the older leaves are affected.”
explain: Only one explanation predicts both symptoms at once. Drought, disease and salt each account for damaged leaves and none of them accounts for a sticky path. The ants are the confirmation: they are there because the honeydew is.

d.story: The young leaves at the tips of the lime tree are curled, and the path beneath it is sticky. Aphids feed on new growth and excrete a sugary liquid called honeydew. a sooty film on three tip branches, and curling before spots
margins that are not browned anywhere
curling confined to this year's shoots alone

“Honeydew falls on whatever is below, which is why the path is tacky.”
args.against: “The water goes on at the trunk and the feeding roots are out at the canopy edge.”

title: The Case of the Pumpkin That Rotted Inward
story: One of the two carved pumpkins collapsed in five days and the other is firm after two weeks. Both were carved on the same afternoon from the same patch and the same size. Both stood side by side on the same step in the same weather. A crack in the shell lets water and spores in, and shows as a line on the outside. Neither pumpkin carries a crack or a soft patch anywhere on its skin. A bruise from dropping shows as a dark sunken spot within a day or two. The candles in both are electric and give off no heat at all. The collapsed one was hollowed quickly and left with pulp and seeds clinging inside. The firm one was scraped down to clean wall with a metal spoon. Wet pulp holds moisture against the cut wall and feeds the moulds that soften it. The collapse began on the inner wall and worked outward to the skin.
q: Why did one pumpkin collapse?

sus.why: the collapsed one was hollowed quickly and left with pulp and seeds clinging inside
neither pumpkin carries a crack or a soft patch anywhere on its skin
a bruise from dropping shows as a dark sunken spot within a day or two
the candles in both are electric and give off no heat at all
both stood side by side on the same step in the same weather

ans: Pulp left inside held moisture against the cut wall.
proof: “Wet pulp holds moisture against the cut wall and feeds the moulds that soften it.”
“The collapse began on the inner wall and worked outward to the skin.”
“The firm one was scraped down to clean wall with a metal spoon.”
clears: A crack: “Neither pumpkin carries a crack or a soft patch anywhere on its skin.”
A bruise: “A bruise from dropping shows as a dark sunken spot within a day or two.”
The candle: “The candles in both are electric and give off no heat at all.”
The weather: “Both stood side by side on the same step in the same weather.”
explain: Three suspects predict damage you could see from outside, and the skin is unmarked on both. The rot ran the other way, inside to out, which points at the one thing that differed: what was left clinging to the inner wall.

“A crack in the shell lets water and spores in and does not show from the front.”

title: The Case of the Prints in the Frost
story: A line of prints crosses the frosted lawn from the hedge to the bins and back. Each print shows four toes and a small triangular pad behind them. A human boot leaves a continuous sole mark with no separate toes at all. These prints are forty millimetres across, far smaller than any boot. Claw marks show clearly in front of every toe in the trail. A cat walks with its claws drawn in and leaves no claw marks in soft frost. A dog's trail runs in two loose lines, with the hind feet landing wide of the front. This trail runs almost in a single line, one print nearly in front of the last. A fox places each hind foot into the print its front foot just left. That habit is what produces a near single line of prints. The stride measures thirty centimetres, which is short for a dog of this foot size. Nothing has disturbed the bin lids and nothing has been dragged across the grass.
q: What made the prints?

sus.why: a fox places each hind foot into the print its front foot just left
a dog's trail runs in two loose lines, with the hind feet landing wide of the front
a cat walks with its claws drawn in and leaves no claw marks in soft frost
a human boot leaves a continuous sole mark with no separate toes at all
nothing has disturbed the bin lids and nothing has been dragged across the grass

ans: A fox crossed the lawn, registering its hind feet in the front prints.
proof: “Claw marks show clearly in front of every toe in the trail.”
“This trail runs almost in a single line, one print nearly in front of the last.”
“That habit is what produces a near single line of prints.”
clears: A dog: “A dog's trail runs in two loose lines, with the hind feet landing wide of the front.”
A cat: “A cat walks with its claws drawn in and leaves no claw marks in soft frost.”
A person: “A human boot leaves a continuous sole mark with no separate toes at all.”
The bins: “Nothing has disturbed the bin lids and nothing has been dragged across the grass.”
explain: Two features have to be explained together. Claws rule out the cat and a single line rules out the dog, and only one animal in the list does both at once. Either feature alone would leave two suspects standing.

d.story: A line of prints crosses the frosted lawn from the hedge to the bins and back. Each print shows four toes and a small triangular pad behind them. Claw marks show clearly in front of every toe in the trail. A fox places each hind foot into the print its front foot just left. That habit is what produces a near single line of prints. This trail runs almost in a single line, one print nearly in front of the last. The stride measures thirty centimetres, which is short for a dog of this foot size. A small dog trotting slowly also sets its feet close to one line. These prints are forty millimetres across, which fits a terrier as well as a fox. A cat chasing something runs with its claws out and leaves marks like these. Two cats live in the terrace and both were out that night. A boot leaves one continuous sole mark and no separate toes. No bin lid has been shifted and nothing has been dragged over the grass.
d.q: What made the prints? Make the case for one animal.

sus.why: a near single line, which is how a fox sets its hind feet
a thirty-centimetre stride, which a small dog can trot
claws out in a chase, and two cats out that night
a boot leaving one continuous sole and no toes
bin lids unshifted and nothing dragged over the grass

evidence: “A fox places each hind foot into the print its front foot just left.”
“This trail runs almost in a single line, one print nearly in front of the last.”
args.against: “A small dog trotting slowly also sets its feet close to one line.”

evidence: “A small dog trotting slowly also sets its feet close to one line.”
“These prints are forty millimetres across, which fits a terrier as well as a fox.”
args.against: “A fox places each hind foot into the print its front foot just left.”

evidence: “A cat chasing something runs with its claws out and leaves marks like these.”
“Two cats live in the terrace and both were out that night.”
args.against: “The stride measures thirty centimetres, which is short for a dog of this foot size.”

clears: A person: “A boot leaves one continuous sole mark and no separate toes.”
Something at the bins: “No bin lid has been shifted and nothing has been dragged over the grass.”
d.note: Claws used to rule the cat out and a chasing cat puts them back in. The single line used to mean fox and a slow trot puts a dog back in. Two pieces of evidence, both weakened by one extra sentence each, which is exactly how real tracking goes.

title: The Case of the Bus That Was Late in the Rain
story: Route 9 runs five minutes late on wet mornings and on time on dry ones. Routes 4 and 11 cover the same main roads and keep to time in any weather. If rain slowed the traffic, all three routes would run late together. The wheelchair lift is used on Tuesdays only, and the late mornings fall on every weekday. Ridership is logged daily and rises by two or three students when it rains. Three extra students board in about twelve seconds, which is not five minutes. The driver's timing sheet shows the whole delay appearing between stops six and eight. Stop seven has no shelter, and the nearest cover is a shop porch across the road. On wet mornings the students wait in that porch and start crossing when the bus appears. Waiting for a group to cross a road takes far longer than letting them step aboard. On dry mornings those same students stand at the pole and board immediately.
q: Why is route 9 late in the rain?

sus.who: 🏪 Students sheltering across the road at stop seven
sus.why: on wet mornings the students wait in that porch and start crossing when the bus appears
if rain slowed the traffic, all three routes would run late together
the wheelchair lift is used on Tuesdays only, and the late mornings fall on every weekday
three extra students board in about twelve seconds, which is not five minutes
the driver's timing sheet shows the whole delay appearing between stops six and eight

ans: At stop seven the students shelter across the road and have to cross.
proof: “Stop seven has no shelter, and the nearest cover is a shop porch across the road.”
“Waiting for a group to cross a road takes far longer than letting them step aboard.”
“On dry mornings those same students stand at the pole and board immediately.”
clears: Traffic: “If rain slowed the traffic, all three routes would run late together.”
The lift: “The wheelchair lift is used on Tuesdays only, and the late mornings fall on every weekday.”
Extra riders: “Three extra students board in about twelve seconds, which is not five minutes.”
The driver: “The driver's timing sheet shows the whole delay appearing between stops six and eight.”
explain: The other two routes are the control for weather and traffic. The timing sheet then narrows five minutes to a single stop, and the only thing that changes at that stop when it rains is which side of the road the students are standing on.

sus.why: a porch across the road, with a group crossing when the bus appears
a station stretch where queues form in rain, missed by the other routes
a lift that runs on Tuesdays alone
nine or ten extra riders, taking over a minute at two stops
one driver since September, running it the same way daily

“On dry mornings those same students stand at the pole and board immediately.”
args.against: “The stretch between stops six and eight runs past the station, where queues form in rain.”

evidence: “The stretch between stops six and eight runs past the station, where queues form in rain.”
“Routes 4 and 11 join the main road after the station and miss that stretch.”

“Nine extra students at two stops take well over a minute to board.”

title: The Case of the Cracked Trophy Base
story: The marble base of the county trophy has split, and the eleven trophies beside it are sound. A fall chips a corner or scuffs an edge before it cracks a base through. There is no chip, scuff or dust mark anywhere on the base or the shelf. Cold and heat craze a stone surface into a web of fine lines across the whole face. These are three clean cracks and there is no crazing anywhere on it. The case is unheated and its temperature log has not moved four degrees all year. The cracks all begin at the bolt hole in the centre and run outward from it. A bolt tightened too far pushes outward on the stone around the hole. Stone takes enormous pressure from above and very little pushing out from inside. The column was refitted in August with a new bolt and a spanner rather than by hand. The eleven sound trophies have never had their columns off.
q: What cracked the base?

sus.why: the column was refitted in August with a new bolt and a spanner rather than by hand
there is no chip, scuff or dust mark anywhere on the base or the shelf
the case is unheated and its temperature log has not moved four degrees all year
the cracks all begin at the bolt hole in the centre and run outward from it
the eleven sound trophies have never had their columns off

ans: A bolt driven in with a spanner split the stone from the hole outward.
proof: “A bolt tightened too far pushes outward on the stone around the hole.”
“Stone takes enormous pressure from above and very little pushing out from inside.”
“The cracks all begin at the bolt hole in the centre and run outward from it.”
clears: A fall: “There is no chip, scuff or dust mark anywhere on the base or the shelf.”
Heat and cold: “These are three clean cracks and there is no crazing anywhere on it.”
The marble: “The cracks all begin at the bolt hole in the centre and run outward from it.”
The shelf: “The eleven sound trophies have never had their columns off.”
explain: Where cracks start is the evidence. A fall starts them at the point of impact and temperature starts them everywhere at once. These start at a hole that had a bolt driven into it, and the eleven trophies that were never taken apart are all intact.

d.story: The marble base of the county trophy has split, and the eleven trophies beside it are sound. Every crack starts at the centre bolt hole and runs outward from there. A bolt tightened too far pushes outward on the stone around the hole. Stone takes enormous pressure from above and very little pushing out from inside. The column was refitted in August with a new bolt and a spanner rather than by hand. The case sits against the radiator wall and its south end reads nine degrees warmer. d.q: Why did the base crack? Pick one cause and back it up.

sus.why: a column refitted in August with a spanner rather than by hand
no chip, scuff or dust mark on the base or the shelf
a south end nine degrees warmer against the radiator wall
a grey vein running straight through the bolt hole
eleven sound trophies that have never had a column off

evidence: “The column was refitted in August with a new bolt and a spanner rather than by hand.”
“A bolt tightened too far pushes outward on the stone around the hole.”
args.against: “This base came from the end of a block and carries a grey vein across its centre.”

evidence: “The case sits against the radiator wall and its south end reads nine degrees warmer.”
“Three clean cracks is what an uneven expansion gives before any crazing appears.”
args.against: “Every crack starts at the centre bolt hole and runs outward from there.”

evidence: “This base came from the end of a block and carries a grey vein across its centre.”
“The vein runs through the bolt hole.”
args.against: “A bolt tightened too far pushes outward on the stone around the hole.”

clears: A fall: “No chip, scuff or dust mark shows on the base or on the shelf.”

title: The Case of the Pale Turkey
story: The turkey came out of the oven cooked through and the colour of raw pastry. The thigh read 176 degrees, so the oven cannot have been running too cool. An oven too cool would have left the meat underdone as well as the skin pale. The bird was rubbed with oil before it went in, so it is not a dry skin. The meat is juicy and the skin is soft rather than dried out. Browning needs a dry surface and heat reaching it directly, and neither was available. The bird was covered with foil at the start and the foil was never taken off. Foil holds steam against the skin for the whole of the roast. A surface held wet cannot brown however long it stays in the oven. The same oven browned a chicken to a deep gold last Sunday. That chicken was roasted uncovered from the first minute to the last.

sus.why: the bird was covered with foil at the start and the foil was never taken off
an oven too cool would have left the meat underdone as well as the skin pale
the bird was rubbed with oil before it went in, so it is not a dry skin
the thigh read 176 degrees, so the oven cannot have been running too cool
the same oven browned a chicken to a deep gold last Sunday

“Foil holds steam against the skin for the whole of the roast.”
“A surface held wet cannot brown however long it stays in the oven.”

No fat: “The bird was rubbed with oil before it went in, so it is not a dry skin.”

The bird: “That chicken was roasted uncovered from the first minute to the last.”
explain: A cooked thigh and a pale skin cannot both be explained by heat or time, because either would have left the meat underdone too. What separates skin from meat is the surface, and the surface spent the whole roast under foil in its own steam.

Uneven batter would put the dark ones in a different place each time. The dark ones appear in the same corner of the oven on every single bake. Rotating the tray halfway through the bake produces an evenly coloured batch. If the tray carried the fault, turning it would simply move the dark side around. An oven with a hot corner browns whatever happens to be sitting in it. The element behind that corner was replaced last term and sits closer to the shelf. The oven thermometer reads nine degrees higher when moved to that corner.

sus.why: an oven with a hot corner browns whatever happens to be sitting in it
a dark tray would brown everything resting on it rather than one corner
uneven batter would put the dark ones in a different place each time
if the tray carried the fault, turning it would simply move the dark side around
the dark ones appear in the same corner of the oven on every single bake

title: The Case of the Mittens That Shrank
story: Two pairs of wool mittens went into the wash the same size and one pair came out child-sized. Both pairs are the same wool from the same maker and the same batch. A fault in the wool would have shrunk both pairs, and one is unchanged. Both were washed in the same machine on the same hot cycle in the same load. Hot water alone swells wool fibres and lets them relax again as they dry. Wool felts when heat and movement act together, because the scales on each fibre lock. Once those scales interlock they cannot be pulled apart and the shrinking is permanent. The shrunken pair went into the tumble dryer on a high heat setting. The unchanged pair was laid flat on a rack and left to dry overnight. A dryer supplies heat and constant tumbling at the same time. Neither pair was stretched, pinned or worn between the wash and the measuring.
q: Why did only one pair shrink?

sus.why: the shrunken pair went into the tumble dryer on a high heat setting
both were washed in the same machine on the same hot cycle in the same load
a fault in the wool would have shrunk both pairs, and one is unchanged
neither pair was stretched, pinned or worn between the wash and the measuring
the unchanged pair was laid flat on a rack and left to dry overnight

ans: The dryer gave heat and tumbling together, which felts wool.
proof: “Wool felts when heat and movement act together, because the scales on each fibre lock.”
“Once those scales interlock they cannot be pulled apart and the shrinking is permanent.”
“A dryer supplies heat and constant tumbling at the same time.”
clears: The hot wash: “Both were washed in the same machine on the same hot cycle in the same load.”
The wool: “A fault in the wool would have shrunk both pairs, and one is unchanged.”
Stretching: “Neither pair was stretched, pinned or worn between the wash and the measuring.”
The rack: “The unchanged pair was laid flat on a rack and left to dry overnight.”
explain: Both pairs got the heat, so heat alone cannot be the answer. Felting needs two things at once, and only one pair met the second. That is why the rule in the story names heat and movement together rather than either on its own.

title: The Case of the Gingerbread That Spread
story: Half the gingerbread figures baked into flat blobs and half held their shape perfectly. Every figure was cut from one bowl of dough mixed and weighed in one go. The second sheet was cut and then chilled for thirty minutes before it went in. The spread figures are all from the first sheet without a single exception. too much baking soda leaves a soapy taste, and these taste exactly as they should
all of them went into the same oven on the same shelf at the same setting
nobody opened the oven door during either bake

title: The Case of the String That Flickered
story: The whole light string flickers together several times a second, all hundred bulbs at once. A loose bulb interrupts its own circuit and flickers that bulb or that half. Every bulb in the string dims and brightens in step, which one loose bulb cannot do. A failing outlet would also affect the lamp plugged into the socket beside it. That lamp has burned steadily in the same socket all evening. These are LED bulbs, which switch on and off far faster than old filament bulbs. The string is plugged into a wall switch fitted with a dimmer last spring. A dimmer chops the current on and off to lower the brightness of a filament lamp. A filament glows through those gaps and an LED follows them exactly. Moving the string to an undimmed socket in the hall stops the flicker completely. Plugging it back into the dimmed switch brings the flicker straight back.
q: Why does the whole string flicker?

sus.why: the string is plugged into a wall switch fitted with a dimmer last spring
every bulb in the string dims and brightens in step, which one loose bulb cannot do
that lamp has burned steadily in the same socket all evening
moving the string to an undimmed socket in the hall stops the flicker completely
plugging it back into the dimmed switch brings the flicker straight back

ans: A dimmer is chopping the current and the LEDs follow every gap.
proof: “A dimmer chops the current on and off to lower the brightness of a filament lamp.”
“A filament glows through those gaps and an LED follows them exactly.”
“Moving the string to an undimmed socket in the hall stops the flicker completely.”
clears: A loose bulb: “Every bulb in the string dims and brightens in step, which one loose bulb cannot do.”
The outlet: “That lamp has burned steadily in the same socket all evening.”
Cold: “Moving the string to an undimmed socket in the hall stops the flicker completely.”
The lead: “Plugging it back into the dimmed switch brings the flicker straight back.”
explain: A hundred bulbs moving in step says the supply is doing it, not any bulb. The dimmer has been there since spring and filament bulbs never showed it, because a filament stays hot through the gaps. The swap test confirms it in both directions.

title: The Case of the Clock That Gained
story: The hall pendulum clock gains four minutes a day, every day, by the same amount. A clock gaining the same amount daily has a pendulum swinging slightly too fast. A pendulum's speed is set by its length and by nothing else that matters here. Shortening a pendulum makes each swing quicker and makes the clock gain. Winding has nothing to do with rate, because the escapement meters the power out. The clock was wound fully on Sunday and gained four minutes that day as usual. Heat lengthens a steel rod and would make this clock lose rather than gain. The hall has been colder, not warmer, since the gaining started in October. The clock was carried to the hall from the office in late September. The bob rests on a nut that is turned to raise or lower it along the rod. A bob carried by the rod swings loose and seats higher when the clock is set down.
q: Why does the clock gain four minutes a day?

sus.why: a bob carried by the rod swings loose and seats higher when the clock is set down
heat lengthens a steel rod and would make this clock lose rather than gain
winding has nothing to do with rate, because the escapement meters the power out
a clock gaining the same amount daily has a pendulum swinging slightly too fast
the hall has been colder, not warmer, since the gaining started in October

proof: “A pendulum's speed is set by its length and by nothing else that matters here.”
“Shortening a pendulum makes each swing quicker and makes the clock gain.”
“The clock was carried to the hall from the office in late September.”

Winding: “The clock was wound fully on Sunday and gained four minutes that day as usual.”
The hall: “The hall has been colder, not warmer, since the gaining started in October.”
The escapement: “A clock gaining the same amount daily has a pendulum swinging slightly too fast.”
explain: Temperature is the trap, because it does change a pendulum and the season did change. It runs the wrong way: a colder hall shortens the rod less, not more. What else happened in late September is the move, and carrying a clock is how a bob ends up seated somewhere new.

if the sun were doing it, the south slopes of all eight would clear together
number 14's chimney was capped years ago and the ring around it is no different from the rest
all eight houses face the same way and get the same hours of sun
rain ran off all eight roofs equally on the night before the snow

The fifteen clean ones are matte card cut from the classroom stock. Rubbing a finger across a fresh line on each kind shows the difference in seconds. The room was dry and the heating had been on since morning.

if the pen were at fault, all twenty-six would have smeared rather than eleven
all twenty-six were stacked together in one pile as soon as they were finished
the room was dry and the heating had been on since morning
all twenty-six were written at the same table within the same twenty minutes

proof: “Gel ink soaks into an absorbent surface and sits on top of a sealed one.”
“Ink that sits on the surface stays wet far longer and wipes with the lightest touch.”
“The fifteen clean ones are matte card cut from the classroom stock.”

title: The Case of the Foam That Would Not Hold
story: The outdoor volcano gushed and flattened in two seconds while the indoor one held a standing foam. Both used the same measured soda and the same bottle of vinegar. A weaker reaction would produce less gas, and the outdoor one fizzed hard and loud. Wind pushes a foam sideways rather than collapsing it where it stands. The air was still enough that a ribbon on the stake barely moved. Carbon dioxide on its own escapes as bubbles that burst the moment they form. A little dish soap gives each bubble a skin that holds it together in a foam. The indoor mixture had a squeeze of dish soap added to the vinegar. The outdoor batch was mixed in a hurry and the soap was left out. Both cones were the same mould and both vents the same width. The outdoor cone shows the same wet ring a strong eruption always leaves.
q: Why did the outdoor foam collapse?

sus.why: the outdoor batch was mixed in a hurry and the soap was left out
the air was still enough that a ribbon on the stake barely moved
a weaker reaction would produce less gas, and the outdoor one fizzed hard and loud
both cones were the same mould and both vents the same width
the outdoor cone shows the same wet ring a strong eruption always leaves

ans: Without soap the gas escaped as bubbles that burst at once.
proof: “Carbon dioxide on its own escapes as bubbles that burst the moment they form.”
“A little dish soap gives each bubble a skin that holds it together in a foam.”
“The indoor mixture had a squeeze of dish soap added to the vinegar.”
clears: Wind: “The air was still enough that a ribbon on the stake barely moved.”
A weak reaction: “A weaker reaction would produce less gas, and the outdoor one fizzed hard and loud.”
The cone: “Both cones were the same mould and both vents the same width.”
The cold: “The outdoor cone shows the same wet ring a strong eruption always leaves.”
explain: The reaction was not the problem and the wet ring proves it: as much gas came out of the outdoor cone as the indoor one. What the outdoor batch had no way of doing was holding that gas, because nothing in it could make a bubble that lasted.

title: The Case of the Crowns That Rubbed Off
story: Gold came off nine crowns onto nine pairs of hands, and the other seventeen are clean. All twenty-six were painted on Monday morning and left on the same rack. All twenty-six had the same two days to dry before they were worn. If drying time were the problem, every crown would mark a hand. None of the twenty-six was sealed with varnish or any other finish. Acrylic paint sets into a plastic film that holds together once it is dry. The nine that rubbed were painted from the gold poster paint pot. The seventeen that did not were painted with the gold acrylic. Both pots were opened the same morning and neither had dried out. Every crown was handled by the same twenty-six students for the same hour.
q: Why did nine crowns rub off?

if drying time were the problem, every crown would mark a hand
a lack of sealant would leave all of them vulnerable rather than nine
both pots were opened the same morning and neither had dried out
all twenty-six were painted on Monday morning and left on the same rack

ans: Poster paint stays soluble and lifts off onto warm hands.
proof: “Poster paint binds with a starch that stays soluble and lifts with warm skin.”
“Acrylic paint sets into a plastic film that holds together once it is dry.”
“The nine that rubbed were painted from the gold poster paint pot.”

title: The Case of the Note That Buzzed
story: One note on the hall piano buzzes, and the eighty-seven others sound clean. A broken string makes a note thin and quiet rather than adding a buzz to it. The buzz also appears faintly when the note an octave below is played. Something lying loose on the soundboard rattles when a note at its own pitch sets the board moving. A nearby note will shake it a little and the octave will shake it less. A two pence coin was found lying flat on the soundboard under the lid.

a broken string makes a note thin and quiet rather than adding a buzz to it
the note has held its pitch exactly against a fork for three weeks
this note stops dead the moment the key comes up, as it should
the buzz also appears faintly when the note an octave below is played

title: The Case of the Kite That Stalled
story: The kite climbs for twenty feet, stops, slides backward and dives into the grass. A kite with too little tail spins on its own axis rather than stalling and sliding back. This kite tracks straight with no spin at all before it stops. Adding two metres of tail changed nothing about the climb or the dive. Wind too strong for a kite pulls hard on the line and then overflies. The line is slack through the whole flight and the meter reads nine miles an hour. The bridle knot sets the angle the kite meets the wind at. A knot too far back tips the nose up until the wind stops flowing over the sail. A sail the wind has stopped flowing over stops lifting and falls backward. The line is new, unkinked and runs freely off the reel. The knot had been slid two centimetres back when the kite was packed away last autumn. Moved forward again to its mark, the kite climbs steadily and stays up.

a kite with too little tail spins on its own axis rather than stalling and sliding back
the line is slack through the whole flight and the meter reads nine miles an hour
this kite tracks straight with no spin at all before it stops
the line is new, unkinked and runs freely off the reel

proof: “The bridle knot sets the angle the kite meets the wind at.”
“A sail the wind has stopped flowing over stops lifting and falls backward.”

The line: “The line is new, unkinked and runs freely off the reel.”

title: The Case of the Yellowing Shamrock
story: The shamrock's lower leaves have yellowed one by one while the top growth stays green. A plant short of water wilts first and its leaf edges go dry and crisp. These leaves are soft and yellow, with no crisp edge anywhere on them. The soil is still wet to the knuckle three days after the last watering. Waterlogged soil fills those gaps, the roots cannot work, and the oldest leaves yellow first. The pot is a decorative one with no drainage hole in the bottom. the new growth is compact and a strong green
waterlogged soil fills those gaps, the roots cannot work, and the oldest leaves yellow first
the plant was repotted into it in September and the yellowing began in October

title: The Case of the Puddle at the Low End

a dead packet would have left all five rows empty rather than one
all five were watered by the same hose for the same count of seconds
the surface of row three is smooth and shows no scratching at all
row three is the one nearest the fence on the south side of the bed

title: The Case of the Egg That Would Not Peel

The six that peeled cleanly came from a carton dated three weeks ago. The six that tore came from a carton collected from the farm on Saturday. Vinegar in the water is said to help, and no vinegar was used on either batch. Cracking an egg before cooling is said to help, and none of the twelve was cracked. all twelve went into the same iced water for the same ten minutes afterward
vinegar in the water is said to help, and no vinegar was used on either batch
cracking an egg before cooling is said to help, and none of the twelve was cracked

title: The Case of the Shadow That Was Too Short
story: The metre stick casts a shadow forty centimetres shorter at school than the same stick casts at home. Both readings were taken at noon on the same day with the same stick. A clock an hour out would move a shadow, but both readings used the same phone. The stick was held against a spirit level and read vertical in both places. A stick leaning away from the sun casts a longer shadow, not a shorter one. The two sites are eleven kilometres apart, which changes the sun's angle by almost nothing. The school stick stood on the sloping tarmac of the car park. A slope tilts the ground the shadow falls on and changes the length it measures. The home stick stood on a patio checked level with the same spirit level. Measured again on level ground at school, the shadow matched the home reading within a centimetre. Both shadows were measured with the same tape from the base of the stick.
q: Why was the school shadow shorter?

a clock an hour out would move a shadow, but both readings used the same phone
a stick leaning away from the sun casts a longer shadow, not a shorter one
the two sites are eleven kilometres apart, which changes the sun's angle by almost nothing
both shadows were measured with the same tape from the base of the stick

ans: The school shadow fell on sloping ground, which shortens it.
proof: “A slope tilts the ground the shadow falls on and changes the length it measures.”
“The home stick stood on a patio checked level with the same spirit level.”

Distance: “The two sites are eleven kilometres apart, which changes the sun's angle by almost nothing.”
The tape: “Both shadows were measured with the same tape from the base of the stick.”
explain: A shadow measurement has three parts: the stick, the sun and the ground. The stick was checked, the sun is the same sun eleven kilometres away, and nobody thought about the ground. Repeating it on level tarmac is the test, and the difference disappears.

the same tubes were fitted when the gym was built in 1998

covering the tip with a small foil cap stopped the bending entirely for a week

the freezer's own temperature log reads a steady minus eighteen all week
that sensor sits at the back of the compartment beside the smooth tub

title: The Case of the Balloon That Burst Alone
story: Twelve balloons were tied along the railing and only the one at the south end burst. All twelve came from one bag and were inflated by the same pump to the same mark. A weak balloon from a bad bag would be as likely to be any of the twelve. The pump has a gauge and every balloon was taken to the same reading. Latex weakens where sunlight falls on it, and weakened latex gives way under pressure. The south end of the railing is the only part in direct sun after eleven o'clock. The other eleven sit in the shade of the building all day. The air inside a balloon in sunlight also warms and pushes outward harder. A thermometer held against the south end balloon read nine degrees above the others. Nothing sharp projects from the railing anywhere along its length. The burst happened at twenty past two, in the hottest part of the afternoon.
q: Why did one balloon burst?

sus.who: ☀️ Direct sun on the south end
sus.why: the south end of the railing is the only part in direct sun after eleven o'clock
a weak balloon from a bad bag would be as likely to be any of the twelve
the pump has a gauge and every balloon was taken to the same reading
nothing sharp projects from the railing anywhere along its length
a thermometer held against the south end balloon read nine degrees above the others

ans: The south end balloon sat in the sun, which weakened it and warmed its air.
proof: “Latex weakens where sunlight falls on it, and weakened latex gives way under pressure.”
“The air inside a balloon in sunlight also warms and pushes outward harder.”
“The burst happened at twenty past two, in the hottest part of the afternoon.”
clears: A weak balloon: “A weak balloon from a bad bag would be as likely to be any of the twelve.”
Over-inflation: “The pump has a gauge and every balloon was taken to the same reading.”
Something sharp: “Nothing sharp projects from the railing anywhere along its length.”
The others: “The other eleven sit in the shade of the building all day.”
explain: The sun does two things here at once, and both push the same way: it weakens the latex from outside and it expands the air from inside. That is why the one balloon in the sun is also the one that goes, and why it goes at the hottest hour rather than the moment it was tied.
